Abstract.

Singular limit problems of reaction-diffusion systems have been studied in cases where the effects of the reaction terms are very large compared with those of the other terms. Such problems appear in literature in various fields such as chemistry, ecology, biology, geology and approximation theory. In this paper, we deal with the singular limit of a general reaction-diffusion system including many problems in the literature. We formulate the problem, derive the limit equation and establish a rigorous mathematical theory.

Key words and phrases: 
Reaction-diffusion system, fast reaction limit, singular limit, nonlinear diffusion problem, degenerate parabolic equation, LpL^{p} convergence.
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification

1. Introduction

Reaction-diffusion systems have long attracted a great deal of attention due to their high expressiveness of spatio-temporal behaviours appearing in chemistry and biology, and the richness of the structure of their solutions. In some problems, systems include reaction terms which are very fast comparing with the other terms. Singular limit of such systems as the reaction rates become extremely large, that is called a fast reaction limit or a instantaneous reaction limit, has been extensively studied in many fields of applications, e.g., diffusive irreversible chemical reactions [7], diffusive reversible chemical reactions [2, 8], spatial segregation of competing species [6, 9], invasion of bacteria in burn wounds [11], reactive solute transport in porous media [18], precipitation and dissolution reaction related to geological disposal of radioactive waste [3], Stefan problem with phase relaxation [27], reaction-diffusion system approximation to degenerate parabolic equations [23], etc. Free boundaries appear in the fast reaction limit of all these problems. By analyzing the fast reaction limit and the ensuing free boundaries, we can understand, e.g., how biological species segregate their habitats, how the barriers that provide safety for geological waste disposal are eroded.

The reaction-diffusion systems in all of the above references can be summarized in the following system:

{∂u∂t=d1​Δ​u+f1​(u,v)−k​F​(u,v)in ​QT:=Ω×(0,T),∂v∂t=d2​Δ​v+f2​(u,v)+c​k​F​(u,v)in ​QT,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=d_{1}\Delta u+f_{1}(u,v)-kF(u,v)&&\mbox{in }Q_{T}:=\Omega\times(0,T),\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=d_{2}\Delta v+f_{2}(u,v)+ckF(u,v)&&\mbox{in }Q_{T},\end{aligned}\right. (1)

where d1d_{1}, d2d_{2} are constants satisfying d1>0d_{1}>0, d2≥0d_{2}\geq 0, and fif_{i} (i=1,2)(i=1,2) and FF are nonlinear functions, a constant cc can be positive or negative, kk is a large positive constant, Ω⊂ℝd​(d∈ℕ)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\ (d\in\mathbb{N}) is a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, TT is a positive constant. The unknown functions u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t), v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) stand for concentrations of chemicals in the cases of chemical reactions and for population densities of species in the case of population ecology at position x∈Ωx\in\Omega and time t∈[0,T)t\in[0,T).

Let us introduce a typical example briefly. Evans [7] considered the following system of diffusive irreversible chemical reactions11 1 Here, we set k:=1/εk:=1/\varepsilon and v:=−vεv:=-v^{\varepsilon}, where ε\varepsilon and vεv^{\varepsilon} are notations used in [7].:

{∂u∂t=d1​Δ​u−k​u​vin ​QT,∂v∂t=d2​Δ​v−k​u​vin ​QT\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=d_{1}\Delta u-kuv&&\mbox{in }Q_{T},\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=d_{2}\Delta v-kuv&&\mbox{in }Q_{T}\end{aligned}\right. (2)

with non-negative initial data. Here, uu and vv denote the concentrations of the two reacting chemicals which combine to form another product. We are interested in the behaviours of the chemicals when the reaction rate kk is very large. Let (uk,vk)(u^{k},v^{k}) be the solution of (2). It has been shown that the limit functions of uku^{k} and vkv^{k} as kk tends to infinity are given by positive z+:=max⁡{z,0}z^{+}:=\max\{z,0\} and negative z−:=max⁡{−z,0}z^{-}:=\max\{-z,0\} parts of the solution zz of the following nonlinear diffusion equation, respectively:

∂z∂t=Δ​β​(z),\frac{\partial z}{\partial t}=\Delta\beta(z), (3)

where β⁡(z):=d1​max​{z,0}+d2​min​{z,0}\beta(z):=d_{1}\max\{z,0\}+d_{2}\min\{z,0\}. This equation (3) is a weak form of a free boundary problem so-called the Stefan problem. The behaviours of the free boundary is well-known and one can estimate the errors between (uk,vk)(u^{k},v^{k}) and (z+,z−)(z^{+},z^{-}) [22]. Therefore, we can understand the behaviours of solutions near the strongly reacting front. This sort of fast reaction limit, especially, with the logistic type of f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}, has been widely studied (see, e.g., [6, 9]).

Like this example, if cc is negative, initial data are non-negative and FF is non-decreasing in both variables with F⁡(a,b)=0F(a,b)=0 iff a​b=0ab=0, then (1) is called irreversible reaction-diffusion system. If cc is positive and F⁡(u,v)F(u,v) is non-decreasing in uu and non-increasing in vv, then (1) is called reversible reaction-diffusion system. The irreversible and the reversible systems have been handled separately because it has been thought that different techniques are required. However, the irreversible system can be written as the reversible system formally by replacing vv with −v-v. Precisely speaking, for F⁡(u,v)=u​vF(u,v)=uv as in (2), F⁡(u,−v)F(u,-v) does not satisfy the monotonicity assumption. If we replace F⁡(u,v)=u​vF(u,v)=uv with

F(u,v)={u​vif u≥0,v≥0,uif u<0,u≤v,vif ​u​<0,u>​v,F(u,v)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &uv&&\mbox{if }u\geq 0,\ v\geq 0,\\ &u&&\mbox{if }u<0,\ u\leq v,\\ &v&&\mbox{if }u<0,\ u>v,\end{aligned}\right.

then F⁡(u,−v)F(u,-v) satisfies the monotonicity assumption and this does not change the dynamics within the invariant set {u,v≥0}\{u,v\geq 0\}. Thus, the reaction-diffusion systems in all of the above references can be reformulated as the reversible system.

In the present paper, we consider the fast reaction limit of the following general system:

{∂u∂t=d1​Δ​u+f1​(u,v)−k​F​(u,v)in ​QT,∂v∂t=d2​Δ​v+f2​(u,v)+k​F​(u,v)in ​QT,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0on ​∂Ω×(0,T),u⁡(0)=u0,v⁡(0)=v0in ​Ω.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=d_{1}\Delta u+f_{1}(u,v)-kF(u,v)&&\mbox{in }Q_{T},\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=d_{2}\Delta v+f_{2}(u,v)+kF(u,v)&&\mbox{in }Q_{T},\\ &\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0&&\mbox{on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\\ &u(0)=u_{0},\quad v(0)=v_{0}&&\mbox{in }\Omega.\end{aligned}\right. (4)

Here, ν\nu is the outward normal unit vector to ∂Ω\partial\Omega and u0u_{0}, v0v_{0} are given initial data. We derive the limit problem as kk tends to infinity and prove the convergence under a broad framework including all of the above references.

Fast reaction limit of three- or multi-component systems have been studied in [10, 12, 14, 24, 25]. The structures of these problems are similar to our framework essentially. In our setting (4), the fast reaction terms in each component uu and vv are represented by the same function FF. Fast reaction limits of systems with different fast reaction terms in equations for uu and vv are still far from being well understood. There are some researches on such problems, see, e.g., [4, 13]. Quite recently, Iida, Ninomiya and Yamamoto reviewed the recent development of fast reaction limits and reaction-diffusion system approximations [15].

The organization of this paper is as follows. In the next section, we state notations and definitions, and give our main results. In Section 3, a priori estimates are provided in L2L^{2} framework. The main result in LpL^{p} (p∈[1,2)p\in[1,2)) space is proved in Section 4. The L∞L^{\infty} estimate and the main result in LpL^{p} (p≥1p\geq 1) space are given in Section 5. Concluding remarks are made in the final section of the paper.

{∂z∂t=Δ​β​(z)+f⁡(z)in ​QT,∂β⁡(z)∂ν=0on ​∂Ω×(0,T),z⁡(0)=u0+v0in ​Ω.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial z}{\partial t}=\Delta\beta(z)+f(z)&&\mbox{in }Q_{T},\\ &\frac{\partial\beta(z)}{\partial\nu}=0&&\mbox{on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\\ &z(0)=u_{0}+v_{0}&&\mbox{in }\Omega.\end{aligned}\right. Our assertion is that the fast reaction limit of (4) is described by the nonlinear diffusion problem (7). Conversely, the solution of the nonlinear diffusion problems of the type (7) can be approximated by a solution of a reaction-diffusion system. In this context, we consider a general initial datum (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) for (7) and its approximation (u0k,v0k)(u_{0}^{k},v_{0}^{k}) as an initial datum of (4). Problem (7) is understood in the following weak sense.

Definition 2.1.

A function z∈L∞​(0,T,L2​(Ω))∩H1​(0,T,H1​(Ω)∗){z}\in L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega))\cap H^{1}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)^{*}) such that β⁡(z)∈L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω)){\beta}({z})\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)) is said to be a weak solution of (7) if it fulfils

−∫0T⟨∂φ∂t,z⟩+∫0T(∇β(z),∇φ)=(u0+v0,φ(0))+∫0T(f(z),φ)-\int_{0}^{T}\left\langle\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t},z\right\rangle+\int_{0}^{T}\left(\nabla\beta({z}),\nabla\varphi\right)=\left(u_{0}+v_{0},\varphi(0)\right)+\int_{0}^{T}\left(f({z}),\varphi\right)

for all functions φ∈L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))\varphi\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)) such that φ⁡(T)=0\varphi(T)=0.

Existence of the weak solution of the nonlinear diffusion equations of type (7) is well-known (see, e.g., [5, 26]). However, uniqueness of the weak solution is not known in general. The weak solution is unique if one of the following additional assumptions holds (see, e.g., [1, 16]):

  • •

    d2>0d_{2}>0,

  • •

    β\beta is strictly monotone,

  • •

    there is a Lipschitz function f~\tilde{f} such that f​(z)=f~​(β​(z))f(z)=\tilde{f}(\beta(z)).

When (10) holds, Assumptions (H2) and (H3) can be weakened. The global Lipschitz continuities of fi​(i=1,2)f_{i}(i=1,2) and FF can be replaced by local Lipschitz continuities, and (6) is not required.

3. A priori estimates

This section is devoted to a priori estimates under Assumptions (H1)–(H4).

Lemma 3.1.

There exists a positive constant CC independent of kk such that

‖uk‖L∞​(0,T,L2​(Ω))∩L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))+‖vk‖L∞​(0,T,L2​(Ω))+d2​‖vk‖L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))≤C.\displaystyle\|u^{k}\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega))\cap L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega))}+\|v^{k}\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega))}+d_{2}\|v^{k}\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega))}\leq C.

Φg​(s)=∫0sg⁡(r)​𝑑rfor ​s∈ℝ.\Phi_{g}(s)=\int_{0}^{s}g(r)dr\qquad\mbox{for }s\in\mathbb{R}.

Let {γδ}δ>0\{\gamma_{\delta}\}_{\delta>0} be a sequence of nondecreasing and Lipschitz continuous functions and γ0\gamma_{0} be a nondecreasing single-valued function such that for all s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}

|γδ​(s)|≤1C1​|s|+C2C1,\displaystyle\left|\gamma_{\delta}(s)\right|\leq\frac{1}{C_{1}}|s|+\frac{C_{2}}{C_{1}}, (12)
γ0​(s)∈α−1​(s),\displaystyle\gamma_{0}(s)\in\alpha^{-1}(s),

Lemma 3.2.

For all u1,u2,v1,v2∈ℝu_{1},u_{2},v_{1},v_{2}\in\mathbb{R}, the following estimate holds.

If u1≥u2u_{1}\geq u_{2} and v1≤v2v_{1}\leq v_{2}, then sgn​(u1−u2)≥sgn​(v1−v2)\mbox{\rm sgn}(u_{1}-u_{2})\geq\mbox{\rm sgn}(v_{1}-v_{2}) and F⁡(u1,v1)≥F⁡(u2,v2)F(u_{1},v_{1})\geq F(u_{2},v_{2}) because of the property of FF. Therefore, the desired estimate holds. In case where u1≤u2u_{1}\leq u_{2} and v1≥v2v_{1}\geq v_{2}, the result is obtained similarly. □\Box

In addition to Assumptions (H1)–(H4), if (10) holds, then the limit functions uu and vv belong to L∞​(QT)L^{\infty}(Q_{T}) and subsequences of {uk}\{u^{k}\} and {vk}\{v^{k}\} converge strongly in Lp​(QT)L^{p}(Q_{T}) for any p≥1p\geq 1.

6. Concluding remarks

In this paper, we have considered the fast reaction limit of (4) under the general setting. Our setting is so general as to include a lot of problems in the literature. The key assumption is the existence of a maximal monotone α\alpha which satisfies (5). Thanks to this, (I+α)−1(I+\alpha)^{-1} is a non-decreasing contraction mapping, and thus, the limit equation (7) is well-defined. The maximal monotonicity assumption of α\alpha might be weakened. If A={(u,v)|v∈α⁡(u)}A=\{(u,v)\ |\ v\in\alpha(u)\} and Bc={(u,v)|u+v=c}B_{c}=\{(u,v)\ |\ u+v=c\} intersect at one point for all c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, the fast reaction limit might be considered. For example, if there exist a constant λ<1\lambda<1 and a multi-valued function α:ℝ→2ℝ\alpha:\mathbb{R}\to 2^{\mathbb{R}} such that α\alpha satisfies (5) and λ​I+α\lambda I+\alpha is maximal monotone, then (I+α)−1=((1−λ)​I+(λ​I+α))−1(I+\alpha)^{-1}=((1-\lambda)I+(\lambda I+\alpha))^{-1} is still non-decreasing and Lipschitz continuous. Therefore, under this assumption, the limit equation (7) is well-defined and one can expect the convergence of the solution of the reaction-diffusion system (4). However, the strategy in this paper can not be applied to this situation. The proof under this assumption remains an open problem. On the other hand, if AA and BcB_{c} intersect at more than two points for some cc, the limit equation (7) is a forward-backward equation, that is, ill-posed. In this case, Turing instability for (4) should occur. The evidences have been obtained for specific choices of FF in (4) [17, 20, 19].
